label: Polynomial Functions
overview: A polynomial function is built from sums of terms with non-negative integer exponents. SAT questions ask you to evaluate polynomials at given inputs, find zeros from factored form, determine the number of solutions from a graph, or match a graph to its equation. Understanding the relationship between factors, zeros, and x-intercepts is central.

keyFormulas.name: Factor from zero
keyFormulas.latex: x = r \text{ is a zero} \iff (x - r) \text{ is a factor}

keyFormulas.name: Degree and end behavior
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Even degree: both ends same direction; Odd degree: opposite directions}

workedExamples.problem: The function f(x) = (x + 3)(x − 1)(x − 5). What are the zeros of f, and for what values of x is f(x) > 0 when x > 5?

steps.title: Find the zeros
steps.content: Set each factor equal to zero.
steps.math: x + 3 = 0 \implies x = -3; \quad x - 1 = 0 \implies x = 1; \quad x - 5 = 0 \implies x = 5

steps.title: Check sign for x > 5
steps.content: Test x = 6: all three factors are positive, so f(6) > 0. Therefore f(x) > 0 for all x > 5.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a zero from the factor as positive when it should be negative
commonMistakes.fix: (x + 3) = 0 gives x = −3, not +3. Set the factor equal to zero and solve.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the y-intercept with the zeros
commonMistakes.fix: Zeros are where the graph crosses the x-axis (y = 0). The y-intercept is found by evaluating f(0).

quickTip: To find the y-intercept of a polynomial quickly, substitute x = 0 into each factor: f(0) = product of all constant terms in each factor.
